sections.html:
The tax code treats your home as a homestead when it is a one-family house you occupy yourself, along with up to 160 acres of land. The house must be your primary residence on the first day of the tax year you are claiming.

Sellers should read that carefully. A vacant house after a move, a rental, or an heir's house when the heirs live elsewhere falls outside it. A house its owner lives in fits, and the owner could get a lower assessed value, with a bigger break for some older and disabled owners. The legal text sits in Title 40 of the Alabama Code, sections 9-19 through 9-21, and the Department of Revenue publishes a homestead page plus yearly memoranda on the income tests.

sections.h2: The homestead types, H-1 through H-4
sections.html:
Act 2013-295 groups Alabama homestead relief into types labeled H-1 through H-4. An owner's age, income and disability status point to the right one.

TypeWho qualifiesBenefit
H-1Under 65 and not disabledTakes $4,000 off assessed value for state tax and $2,000 off for county tax
H-2Age 65 or older with adjusted gross income below $12,000 on the latest state return, or retired for permanent and total disabilityNo state tax, plus $5,000 off assessed value for county tax, school district tax included
H-3 (age 65+)Age 65 or older with net taxable income of $12,000 or less on the combined federal returnNo ad valorem tax at all
H-3 (disabled)Permanently and totally disabledNo ad valorem tax at all, whatever the income
H-4Age 65 or older with income over $12,000 on the latest Alabama returnNo state tax, plus the usual $2,000 assessed-value exemption on county taxes

Keep in mind these numbers refer to assessed value, not what a house sells for. Residential property is assessed at only a fraction of market value, which means a small assessed-value cut wipes out a far larger piece of the sale price from taxation.

Each piece of the bill, whether state, county or school district, gets its own relief, so a pair of neighbors who differ in age can pay very different amounts.

State tax first: anyone under 65 gets up to $4,000 of assessed value off, with no income test. Those 65 or older, the permanently and totally disabled, and blind owners face no cap on the state exemption and no income test, under the same 160-acre ceiling.

Counties vary more. A county, a municipality or another taxing authority can add an exemption of its own worth up to $4,000 in assessed value, and county school tax applies to some owner categories but not others. The result depends on where the house is and who owns it. To learn what a buyer would owe, phone the local assessing office rather than assuming the statewide minimum.

Go to your county office, not the state. Apart from public utility property, every property tax is assessed and collected by one of the 67 county tax offices.

  • Show that you own the house and that it is your primary residence.
  • For an age-based type, bring proof of age, and the return named in that year's memorandum if there is an income limit.
  • For disability, a doctor fills out a physician's affidavit confirming permanent and total disability.
  • Ask which type the office has on file for you.

The Revenue Department's site lists county contacts. If you are unsure which office handles your parcel, the Property Tax Division answers at 334-242-1525.

Title 40, section 9-21 adds a combined state, county and city principal residence exemption. Two groups qualify: people 65 or older whose income on the combined federal return is $12,000 or less, and the permanently and totally disabled of any age.

Both groups get no maximum assessed value, a 160-acre land limit, and no county school tax. The disabled category has no income limit. The relief closely matches what the H-3 type describes.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption when you sell
sections.html:
Nothing here lets you guess about a mid-year sale, so ask the county. The firm rule is occupancy: you must live in the home as your primary residence on the first day of the tax year.

In practice the test splits things. Had you lived there that day, your exemption for the year rested on that, and a later buyer who moves in begins with the county office. An investor who will rent or flip the house cannot meet the test, so an investor should price the property assuming full tax.

  • Ask the county how your sale date changes this year's bill.
  • Read the title company's statement to see how tax is divided between buyer and seller.
  • Save your exemption approval letter for the title company.

Heirs who do not live in an inherited house fall outside the occupancy wording, so assume the decedent's exemption has ended. When the earlier owner was 65 or older and paid little or no tax, the next bill can come as a shock.

Payment is due October 1, delinquency starts after December 31, and the County Revenue Commissioner need not mail a notice. A slow estate can let a bill go unpaid and grow into a bigger problem, so look at the account early.

Some heirs sell as is to avoid repairs, carrying costs and open questions. A cash buyer can close when you are ready and deal with the cleanup, which ends the tax clock running against you. Take your time comparing options, and decline any offer at no cost.

A short timetable governs the tax cycle. An exemption shrinks the amount owed but leaves every date where it is.

  • October 1 is when payment is due.
  • January 1 begins delinquency.
  • February sends unpaid accounts to the probate court.
  • March is when that court meets.
  • April brings advertising of the property for sale.
  • May is the tax sale.

Add the day you list or sign a sales contract, since that date affects how the bill is split.

Manufactured homes follow one different rule: owners over 65 skip the registration fee on an owner-occupied manufactured home, but they still pay the $5 issuance fee.

It sits apart from the homestead types and matters if you sell a manufactured home on land you own. The home and the land can be billed differently, so ask the county which fees and exemptions go with each.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the Alabama homestead exemption?
faqs.a: You do if you own a one-family house, live in it as your primary residence on day one of the tax year, and hold up to 160 acres. How much you get depends on age, income and disability, across types H-1 to H-4.

faqs.q: How much is the basic exemption for owners under 65?
faqs.a: An H-1 owner receives $4,000 off assessed value for state tax and $2,000 off for county tax. Counties and other taxing authorities can add up to $4,000 of their own.

faqs.q: Do I apply with the state or the county?
faqs.a: At the county office. The state writes the rules, while counties do the assessing and collecting.

faqs.q: When are Alabama property taxes due?
faqs.a: They come due October 1 and turn delinquent after December 31. Because the County Revenue Commissioner need not mail a bill, the tax is owed even if no statement shows up.

faqs.q: Can I keep my homestead exemption after I sell?
faqs.a: Check with the county about a mid-year sale. Your buyer applies on their own, and the occupancy test asks who lives in the house on the first day of the tax year.
